items.title: Announcing New vLLM and SGLang Inference Engines on TPU
items.summary: This post announces native PyTorch backends for vLLM and SGLang powered by TorchTPU, enabling developers to run and optimize serving workloads using familiar PyTorch tools. Built in collaboration with open-source project maintainers, these engines include optimized TPU kernel implementations, production-ready features like KV cache management with TPU Sync, and disaggregated serving. Public benchmarks demonstrate state-of-the-art performance and industry-leading cost efficiency on Ironwood TPU across long-context and agentic workloads.

items.title: Preview, edit, and collaborate on markdown (.md) files natively in Google Docs and Drive

This integration preserves native file fidelity for use with Git repositories and developer tools while unlocking standard Docs features like line-level commenting, rendered Drive previews, and tracked version history.

The framework helps engineers organize their guides and solutions to effectively share AI-driven conversational interface designs with the developer community.

items.summary: The Agents CLI Extension System enables developers to use frameworks like LangChain, LangGraph, or custom enterprise stacks while retaining a unified deployment and evaluation workflow. It details a first-party LangChain template that scaffolds, runs, and deploys agents without requiring the Agent Development Kit (ADK). Additionally, it demonstrates how platform teams can author custom extensions to enforce policies such as automated software bill of materials (SBOM) scans during deployment.

items.title: Integrating TorchTPU into TorchTitan and Optimizing Models for TPU
items.summary: TorchTPU integrates a native torch.device("tpu") backend directly into PyTorch, allowing developers to train large-scale models on Google Cloud TPUs without rewriting code in JAX. Developers can leverage these battle-tested optimization playbooks, recipes, and the Hugging Face modeling backend to efficiently scale their own workloads on TPU infrastructure.

items.title: Fast, reliable A2UI, with swappable inference formats
items.summary: A2UI now supports swappable inference formats, introducing A2UI Express which uses up to 3x fewer tokens and cuts latency by compiling compact Python-style syntax into standard A2UI JSON via Agent SDKs. Developers can also use controlled generation with TypeSafe's Jev system-decision models to render known-shape screens in under 300 ms while smaller models stream text. These updates require no changes to frontend renderers or component catalogs, offering flexible performance levers for generative UI development across Python, TypeScript, and Dart.

Developers can use streaming tools to yield progress updates or background execution patterns to keep conversations fluid during long-running backend queries. Additionally, configuring response scheduling behaviors such as WHEN_IDLE, INTERRUPT, or SILENT gives developers precise control over when and how tool results are delivered into the conversation.

items.title: Bringing Visual Graph Debugging to Custom Edge Compilers with Model Explorer
items.summary: Google AI Edge Model Explorer now supports custom compiler intermediate representations and open-source adapters like TOSA, VGF, and PTE for on-device machine learning. Developers can leverage hierarchical graph visualization, split-pane views, and per-node trace overlays to catch export regressions and verify hardware delegation. These tools enable engineering teams to transparently debug execution graphs and pinpoint cycle-level latency bottlenecks locally.

items.title: Announcing DPoP Support for Google OAuth: Securing Refresh Tokens
items.summary: Google OAuth Platform now supports DPoP (Demonstrating Proof-of-Possession) to sender-constrain refresh tokens, neutralizing Infostealer malware and adversary-in-the-middle attacks. By cryptographically binding long-lived refresh tokens while maintaining short-lived access tokens as standard Bearer tokens, developers achieve robust credential security without incurring high-QPS API performance overhead. Additionally, developers integrating multi-agent or Model Context Protocol (MCP) workloads can use Google Cloud Secure Token Service (STS) to handle secure token delegation across agent chains.

items.title: Three ways a calendar tells you what changed
items.summary: Sooner or later, every app that shows a user's calendar wants its own copy of it. You want to search events in your database, join them with your own data, and show a week without waiting on three slow APIs. So you copy the calendar into a table, and then you have the real problem: keeping that table correct without downloading the whole calendar every five minutes. Google Calendar, Microsoft Outlook and CalDAV servers like iCloud can all tell you "here's what changed since last time". They just do it in three quite different ways, and each one breaks in its own way. Here's what I learned wiring up all three. Google has the cleanest model. You list a calendar's events once with no filters, follow pageToken through every page, and the last page hands you a nextSyncToken: GET /calendar/v3/calendars/primary/events?maxResults=2500 { "items": [ ... ], "nextPageToken": "CiAKGjBpNDd2..." } ... { "items": [ ... ], "nextSyncToken": "CPDAlvWDx70CEPDAlvWDx70CGAU=" } Next time, you send that token back and get only what changed since then. items.title: Finding a free slot across Google, Outlook and iCloud
items.summary: Here's a feature request that sounds like an afternoon's work: show the times when Ana (on Google Calendar) and Raj (on Outlook) are both free for 30 minutes next week, during Berlin working hours. You fetch two lists of busy times, merge them and look for the gaps. The merge really is the easy part. The hard part is getting a busy time you can trust from each provider, because the three big calendar APIs each answer "when is this person busy?" in a different way, and one of them barely answers it at all. Google is the easy one. You POST /freeBusy with a window and a list of calendar ids, and get back busy ranges per calendar: { "calendars": { "primary": { "busy": [{ "start": "2026-11-09T08:30:00Z", "end": "2026-11-09T09:00:00Z" }] }, "team@example.com": { "errors": [{ "domain": "global", "reason": "notFound" }] } } } There are two things to notice. First, Google has already applied its own rules: an event marked "show as free" (transparency: "transparent") isn't in there, and it works for calendars the user can only see as free/busy, where listing events would give you nothing. items.title: One standup, three calendar APIs
items.summary: A daily standup is the most boring event on any calendar. It's also where calendar APIs disagree the most. Here's the event I'll use for the rest of this post: a standup at 9:30 in Berlin, every weekday, ten times, starting Monday, November 9. Someone cancels Tuesday's. Someone else moves Friday's to 10:00. Any calendar UI can show that in a second, but each of the three big APIs stores it in its own way, and an app that supports all three has to read and write every version. I've spent a lot of time with these differences while building calsdk, so here is how each provider stores that week, and the places where it caught me out. Google is the closest to the standard. items.title: Server-Sent Events in Node.js: A Real-Time Dashboard That Survives Reconnects
items.summary: Most real-time dashboard demos stop at the happy path: new EventSource('/events'), a chart, done. Then a laptop switches Wi-Fi networks, the stream drops for a second, and the chart quietly skips a few dozen points. Nobody notices until the dashboard totals stop matching the database. Server-sent events (SSE) already include most of what you need to avoid that: event ids, automatic reconnection, and a Last-Event-ID header the browser sends when it reconnects. The browser side comes for free. The server side is up to you, and that is where the gaps usually are. In this post we build a small real-time analytics dashboard on plain Node.js (no framework, no npm runtime dependencies) and make it hold up under real failures: Write the text/event-stream format correctly (multi-line data, ids, retry). Keep the stream alive through proxies with heartbeat comments. Replay missed events after a reconnect, using Last-Event-ID and a bounded event log. Stop one slow client from eating the server’s memory (backpressure). Render at most once per animation frame, however fast events arrive. items.title: Discord Is Ditching Electron For Rust
items.summary: Discord is replacing Electron with a desktop client built fully in Rust, which the company says should significantly reduce the app's notoriously high resource usage while improving performance and memory safety. "We've been early adopters of Rust since 2018 and a lot of our infra, voice tech, and even some of the current client is already Rust, the holy grail was getting the whole client there," explains Discord chief technology officer Stanislav Vishnevskiy in a post on X. "That means Electron goes away, and so does React Native, mobile keeps native UI but shares app code with desktop via Rust." The Verge reports: Vishnevskiy also shared an image of the Discord Windows client using just 290MB of RAM, which is a clear improvement as you only have to participate in a few servers and RAM usage can easily hit 1GB or more using the current Windows app. It's not clear when Discord will make the full switch over to Rust, but Vishnevskiy says the company "hope to get it into testing with users soon." Read more of this story at Slashdot.

Reusing player-42/loading-screen.png is not a harmless convenience: the second attempt can replace the first output before you know which job succeeded. Short answer: write every render attempt to a unique key, keep prompt and job state in your database, and copy the winning object to a canonical key only after the database transaction commits. Object storage without versioning cannot recover an accidental overwrite by itself. The failure usually looks like a missing image, but the first question is whether it was ever missing. A worker may generate image A, upload it, time out while acknowledging the upload, and retry the same job. The retry creates image B at the same key. If the database still points at A's render record, a later cleanup task can delete the object that B now occupies. From the database's perspective, the image vanished; from storage's perspective, two writes simply targeted one name. I have seen this class of incident produce a clean 200 from the upload path and a confusing 404 from the later read, because the application had already deleted the key it thought belonged

items.title: I built Quasnooze, a local-by-default personal AI assistant in plain Node.js 22 with zero runtime dependencies
items.summary: Over the past few weeks I have been building Quasnooze, an MIT-licensed personal AI assistant designed to run on your own machine without pulling in a massive dependency tree or hiding its behavior behind prompts. Most assistant projects I tried either required Docker plus hundreds of npm packages or trusted a system prompt not to do anything destructive. I wanted the opposite: something small enough to read end to end, honest about what it can and cannot do, and strict about permissions in actual code. A few things that came out of building it this way: Zero mandatory runtime dependencies. Everything runs on the Node.js 22+ standard library in plain ESM with no TypeScript and no build step. That meant writing things like the Discord gateway RFC 6455 WebSocket client, SSE token streaming, and incremental BM25 workspace document search directly on Node built-ins. A fresh clone runs right away, and npm run demo boots a local canned brain in about two seconds with no Ollama install or API keys needed. Local by default, explicit boundaries everywhere else. items.summary: Book: TypeScript Essentials Also by me: The TypeScript Library — the 5-book collection My project: Hermes IDE | GitHub — an IDE for developers who ship with Claude Code and other AI coding tools Me: xgabriel.com | GitHub You write the check: if (status). On the next line you pass an arrow function to setTimeout, and inside it the editor underlines status.length with 'status' is possibly 'undefined'. You just checked. The compiler saw you check. It still won't take your word for it. TypeScript is answering a question you didn't ask yourself: when does that arrow function run? Sometimes the answer is "after the value changed", and then the compiler is right. Sometimes the answer is "after nothing can change it anymore", and for years the compiler flagged those cases too. TypeScript 5.4, released on March 6, 2024, fixed the second group. Not all of it, though, and the cases it left alone all have a recognizable shape. Narrowing is control-flow analysis. items.title: Building a nationwide court directory for Mexico from OpenStreetMap
items.summary: We needed a list of every place to play padel, tennis and pickleball in Mexico. Nobody sells a good one, so we built it from OpenStreetMap, and learned that an open map is a mirror of the people who edited it. MeetAndPlay is a padel, tennis and pickleball app that launches in Cancún on 1 December 2026. An app that helps people find a game needs to know where the courts are, in a country with 32 states and a lot of places that never made it into a booking platform. We built a nationwide directory, the court directory at meetandplay.mx/canchas, on top of OpenStreetMap. This post covers the pipeline, the licence, and the quality problems we found, with the real numbers from our latest snapshot. The alternatives were scraping a booking marketplace, buying a commercial POI dataset, or using a map provider's places API. We rejected each for a different reason: terms of service, price, and licences that forbid storing and re-publishing the data. items.title: Streamlining Full-Stack Development: A Monorepo Approach with Next.js and Node.js
items.summary: Streamlining Full-Stack Development: A Monorepo Approach with Next.js and Node.js Modern full-stack web applications demand tight cohesion between frontend interfaces and backend microservices. In traditional multi-repository setups, frontend and backend teams face continuous friction: duplicated TypeScript interfaces, out-of-sync API contracts, disparate linting rules, and disjointed deployment cycles. A simple database schema change often requires three separate pull requests, coordinated npm package publishing, and fragile version pinning. Adopting a unified Monorepo architecture powered by Turborepo and pnpm fundamentally eliminates this overhead. In a monorepo, your Next.js frontend, Node.js API services, and shared libraries (Zod schemas, UI components, utility logic) live together in a single repository. You gain atomic cross-stack commits, instantaneous type inference across network boundaries, and lightning-fast incremental builds powered by computation caching. In this comprehensive guide, we build a production-grade full-stack monorepo from scratch. items.title: Node.js Email Webhooks Need an Idempotency Ledger
items.summary: Email verification becomes a different problem once delivery is asynchronous. The browser submits a form, a provider sends a message, and your app receives one or more webhook events later. If the webhook handler simply activates the user on every event, a retry can create duplicate work or move the account into the wrong state. I like treating the webhook as an event stream with a small idempotency ledger. It gives a Node.js service one reliable place to answer three questions: have I seen this event, what did I do with it, and is this event still allowed to change the user? Thats more useful than adding another retry around a flaky request. The same design helps when a team uses a burner email generator or a disposable email address generator for test fixtures. Test inboxes can make delivery behavior visible, but only an event record can make replays safe. Providers retry webhooks for normal reasons: your endpoint timed out, a network connection closed after the response was sent, or a deploy briefly interrupted traffic. items.title: How to Build SMS-Based OTP in Node.js with Third-Party APIs: Reliability
items.summary: Short answer: to implement SMS-based OTP in Node.js using third-party APIs for two-factor authentication, keep the verification decision in your application and treat SMS delivery as an external, observable step. Generate and send the OTP through a specialist verification API or a general communications API, record the provider request ID, expose resend as a bounded state transition, and alert on the point where a user cannot finish signup rather than on every transient carrier delay. The practical choice is a reliability boundary, not a provider popularity contest. Infrai is a reasonable fit when one REST discovery surface and one credential should cover this SMS operation alongside other backend capabilities; a dedicated verification product is the better choice when fraud controls, regional sender policy, and verification analytics are the product. The incident page should read like a user journey: signup verification completion has fallen, resend attempts are rising, and the pending-verification age is crossing its service objective. items.title: Launch HN: Rivet (YC W23) – Scale and Orchestrate Agents on S3
items.summary: Hey HN, this is Nathan and Nicholas from Rivet (https://rivet.dev) – a fast, high-density, and scalable orchestrator for agentic workloads using the actor model. Rather than running a heavyweight sandbox per agent, each agent gets a lightweight actor backed by S3. Actors provide a long-lived process for long agent turns, in-memory state for context, a WebSocket server for multiplayer, durable SQLite storage backed by S3, and hibernation when idle. It's a similar model to Cloudflare Durable Objects, but it’s open source and self-hostable. Here’s a video walkthrough: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=3Ev6I7DOV9c When we went through YC in 2023, we were building infrastructure for multiplayer games like Diep and Krunker. This involved heavily optimizing high-throughput matchmaking, real-time player messages, and blitz scaling. Through that process, we spent a lot of time on workloads where Postgres couldn't keep up with our throughput. We started out by hacking together Lua scripts on top of Redis, but this became too cumbersome to maintain and upgrade. items.title: Making a SwiftUI app survive a folding iPhone: what broke on the iPhone Duo and how I fixed it
items.summary: I make PawLife, a small pet health app (feeding plans in grams, a health diary, a food safety lookup). It is one SwiftUI codebase for iPhone, iPad, Mac Catalyst, Apple Watch and visionOS. When Xcode 27.2 shipped simulators for the iPhone Duo, I expected "it is just a wider iPhone". It is not. Here is what actually broke, in the order I found it, and what the fixes looked like. The Duo has an outer display and an inner one across the fold. Your app runs on one of them at a time, and the window changes size when the user folds or unfolds. The simulator reports it as a window resize, not a new scene. Measured on the simulator: Folded: a 466×678 pt window, of which my app got 382 pt of width. The remaining 84 pt on the trailing edge is a reserved column (status area and camera) exposed through the safe area. Open: a landscape 951×669 pt window, 867 pt for the app, with the same 84 pt trailing column. So the app goes from a narrow portrait phone to a wide landscape slab and back, live, without a relaunch. Provider Downtime: When an upstream provider experiences elevated latencies or 503 outages, the entire application grinds to a halt. items.title: LISTEN/NOTIFY performance in PostgreSQL
items.summary: I'm building Corfedo Work, a .NET library for background jobs that keeps its state in the application's own PostgreSQL database. Its workers need to know when something changed: a job became due, or a job somebody is waiting for has ended. The PostgreSQL answer is NOTIFY in the transaction that made the change. I designed the library's signals around it. Then I measured it. Single-row transactions with a NOTIFY committed about 3,900 times per second with 8 clients, and about 3,900 with 64. Without the NOTIFY, the same transactions reached 16,700 and 56,700. A signal in Work says "something you wait for may have changed, read again". It's a topic and a key, with no data. items.title: iOS silent push not working: content-available and background pushes
items.summary: A silent push, which Apple calls a background notification, has no alert, sound or badge. It wakes your app so it can fetch new content. Apple treats it as low priority and does not guarantee delivery, so "it worked once and then stopped" is often the system working as designed. This page goes through what must be right on the sender and in the app, and what the device itself decides. What you see Likely cause Fix Never arrives, alert pushes work Remote notifications background mode not ticked Signing and Capabilities > Background Modes > Remote notification Shows a banner instead of waking the app quietly alert, sound or badge in aps next to content-available Send aps with content-available: 1 and nothing else APNs returns 400 apns-priority: 10 with apns-push-type: background Priority 5 for background pushes, always Delivered late, or in bursts Priority 5 pushes are sent according to the device's power state Expected; use an alert push for anything a person waits for Arrives in testing, then stops Throttled: too many background pushes Two or three an hour at most Nothing after the user swiped the app away The app was force quit Nothing to fix; it wakes again once the user opens it

items.summary: Agents love “fixing” forms. items.title: Laravel CORS Error with React or Vue: Causes and Fixes
items.summary: You split the project in two: Laravel serves an API on localhost:8000, and a React or Vue app runs on localhost:5173. The first request from the browser fails, and the console shows a message along these lines (Chrome's wording): Access to fetch at 'http://localhost:8000/api/users' from origin 'http://localhost:5173' has been blocked by CORS policy: No 'Access-Control-Allow-Origin' header is present on the requested resource. The API itself is usually fine. CORS is a browser rule: the browser asks the server whether a page from another origin may read its response, and the server answers with headers. Laravel already has the machinery for that answer. Most fixes are a few lines of config, and I checked each one against the real middleware. Two URLs have the same origin only if scheme, host and port all match. localhost:5173 and localhost:8000 differ in the port, so every request between them is cross-origin. The server never blocks anything. It sends Access-Control-* headers, and the browser decides whether your JavaScript may see the response. items.summary: Processing PDFs entirely on the client side is becoming the gold standard for modern web applications. It provides zero-latency interactions, eliminates expensive backend compute (no headless Chrome or Ghostscript clusters), and guarantees 100% data privacy since documents never leave the user's browser sandbox. However, once you move from toy examples to handling real-world 50MB+ PDFs, you inevitably encounter three major bottlenecks: Silent Memory Leaks: Generating visual thumbnails in easily spikes tab memory past 1.5GB, crashing mobile and low-spec machines. Text Degradation: Many naive implementations convert pages into raster images, causing selectable vector glyphs to turn into blurry bitmaps. Strict Binary Parser Failures: pdf-lib is brilliant for lossless stream operations, but it strictly enforces PDF standards. When a user uploads a slightly malformed or non-compliant document, it throws Error: Expected instance of PDFDict, breaking the workflow. While HTML provides the structure of a webpage and CSS controls its appearance, JavaScript adds functionality and interactivity. For example, an e-commerce website can dynamically display product filters, shopping cart updates, and search suggestions. items.title: Romanian CNP Validator in TypeScript, Zod and React
items.summary: TL;DR A Romanian CNP validator checks five things: 13 digits, a first digit from 1 to 9, a birth date that exists and is not in the future, a county code (01 to 48, 51, 52, or 70, which the new civil status system has used since May 2024) and the check digit. The check digit is the sum of the first 12 digits multiplied by the matching digits of 279146358279, mod 11, with a remainder of 10 written as 1. Store a valid CNP encrypted, with a keyed hash for lookups, because a plain SHA-256 of one can be brute forced in about half an hour on one CPU core. Your checkout, payroll or rental contract form asks for a Romanian personal numeric code (CNP), and a 13-digit regex accepts every typo. A Romanian CNP validator has to check more than the length: a digit for sex and century, a birth date that exists, a county code and a weighted check digit. This tutorial writes that check in TypeScript, decodes the parts, turns it into a zod rule and a React field that validates as you type, and ends with what to do before you store a single CNP. items.title: How we built a RabbitMQ desktop client with Electron, tRPC and SQLite
items.summary: Introduction RabbitGUI is a desktop client for RabbitMQ that runs on macOS, Windows and Linux. It is built with Electron, and this article explains how the pieces fit together. The main process talks to RabbitMQ, exposes everything to the UI through a typed tRPC API, and stores messages in a local SQLite database. The renderer is a plain React app that never touches the network or the disk itself. If you are building a developer tool on Electron, most of this applies to you too. None of it is specific to RabbitMQ. RabbitMQ already ships a web UI, the management plugin. We could have built another web app on top of the same HTTP API. We didn't, for three reasons: A browser can't speak AMQP. The management HTTP API is fine for listing queues and reading stats, but the interesting features need a real AMQP 0-9-1 connection over a raw TCP socket: consuming a whole queue, spying on live traffic, republishing thousands of messages with throttling. Browsers only get TCP through WebSockets, which would need an extra plugin on the broker. A Node.js process gets TCP sockets out of the box. No server in the middle. items.title: Form validation patterns that catch errors early and stay accessible
items.summary: Bad form validation feels like a wall: red text everywhere, fields resetting, cryptic errors, and no clear path to "fix it". Good validation feels like a guide, catching mistakes early, explaining clearly what's wrong, and supporting different input methods and devices. Catch errors early, not late: Validate as users type or on blur, not only on submit. Explain in plain language: No jargon or backend error messages exposed. items.title: 5 Mistakes That Make a Hosted Code Interpreter Lie to Your Users
items.summary: Demo day. Someone drops HostedCodeInterpreterTool into ChatOptions.Tools, uploads a CSV, and the model returns a clean summary with a chart. Applause. Then staging: the same tool list, fluent prose, zero CodeInterpreterToolCallContent. Another run ships a .exe-shaped artifact "so the user can see what was blocked." A third treats a hosted file id the model never downloaded as grounded evidence. The marker did its job. Policy did not. HostedCodeInterpreterTool in Microsoft.Extensions.AI is a marker (name code_interpreter). Capable backends may run a sandbox. The class does not enforce MIME allowlists, byte caps, secret shapes, or hash binding. Prefer the Responses path (GetResponsesClient().AsIChatClient() or equivalent) so CodeInterpreterToolCallContent / CodeInterpreterToolResultContent surface cleanly. This post is five mistakes I keep seeing — idea, why it hurts, skeleton of the fix. Snippets are truncated on purpose. Tech Skill Builder is $5/month for a very limited time only (normally $10). items.title: Understanding SwiftUI's layoutPriority: HStack, ZStack, and Custom Layouts
items.summary: SwiftUI makes building interfaces straightforward, but its layout system can sometimes produce unexpected results. One modifier that developers often reach for is .layoutPriority(). For example: swift This can help resolve layout issues, but what exactly does the priority value mean? And does the modifier behave the same way in every container? To explore these questions, I built an interactive open-source project called SwiftUI Layout Lab. The .layoutPriority() modifier provides a priority value that parent layouts can use when determining how to size their children. The default priority is 0. A higher priority doesn't directly specify a width, height, or percentage of available space. Its effect depends on the parent layout algorithm and the sizing behavior of the child views. For example, assigning a priority of 100 doesn't mean a view will receive 100 times more space than a view with priority 1. An HStack arranges views horizontally, but what happens when there isn't enough space for every view to receive its preferred width? In Layout Lab, you can: Select one of three views. Change its layout priority. Adjust the available container width. Observe the actual measured widths.

items.summary: Last week's client was Go: a 5.8 MB static binary that starts in under two milliseconds, which is a high bar for any language with HTTP in its standard library. This week it's C#. .NET has had everything the spec needs in the box for a decade, and since .NET 8 it has had Native AOT, which compiles the whole program to a single native executable with no runtime to install. I wanted to know whether that gets a C# client anywhere near Go on size and cold start. It gets closer than I expected, though the runtime column on the leaderboard shows what the binary size leaves out. The code is at github.com/AndyCross/claude-hot-path, and the spec every client passes is at /claude-hot-path/. For a client this small I went the other way and used JsonNode, the DOM API, because the request body and the event payloads are built and read dynamically anyway and a context class would have doubled the file. items.title: I Changed object to Lock and Stopped Paying the Monitor Tax
items.summary: I had a counter behind a lock that a profiler kept flagging, and I couldn't figure out why. The lock was basically never contended. One thread wrote to it almost all the time; the lock was there for the rare second writer that might show up. So I expected it to cost close to nothing. It didn't cost nothing. It cost about 24 nanoseconds every single acquire, and on a hot path that adds up to a line you can see in a flame graph. The thing I'd stopped thinking about is what lock (someObject) actually compiles to. It's Monitor.Enter and Monitor.Exit wrapped in a try/finally, and Monitor hangs its state off the object's sync block. Even with no contention at all, you pay for that bookkeeping on every acquire and release. For years that was just the price of the lock keyword and there was nothing to do about it. Since .NET 9 there is. There's a real type now, System.Threading.Lock, and the compiler special-cases it: if you lock on a variable whose type is Lock, it doesn't go through Monitor at all. It calls the type's own fast path instead. The part that surprised me is how little the code changes. // before private readonly object _gate = new(); lock (_gate) { _count++; } // after priva

Strong typing. Managed memory. A sophisticated compiler. A comprehensive runtime. The kind of language that wears a suit to work. It also has some really weird behavior hiding beneath that professional exterior. But before we get into that, a little history. C# arrived in 2002 as part of Microsoft's original .NET Framework, an ecosystem closely associated with Windows and Microsoft's proprietary development tools. For years, C# was the language many developers associated with enterprise Windows applications, corporate IT departments, and Visual Studio. Then something unexpected happened. Microsoft embraced open source. .NET Core arrived in 2016 as an open-source, cross-platform implementation. In 2020, .NET 5 dropped the "Core" name, establishing the modern .NET platform. items.title: How to Manage Python Dependencies Natively inside C# Build Pipelines
items.summary: Python has a massive ecosystem of AI, machine learning, and data science libraries like PyTorch, NumPy, and Transformers. While libraries like PythonNET allow us to call Python from C#, managing the underlying environment setup can be tedious: Installing CPython runtimes across different target environments Restoring pip packages and virtual environments Managing module search paths (sys.path) and native .dll/.so binaries To streamline this workflow, I built DotNetPip, an open-source MSBuild integration that handles Python dependency resolution directly inside your standard .csproj build target. Instead of running external environment setup scripts, you declare your Python packages directly inside your project file: When you run dotnet build, custom MSBuild tasks trigger behind the scenes to: Add the DotNetPip package from NuGet: dotnet add package DotNetPip Declare your required Python dependencies in your .csproj. Run dotnet build The goal is to make using Python's AI/ML ecosystem feel like a first-class citizen inside the .NET toolchain without manual sidecar scripts. items.title: Day 12: Cross-Node Invalidation for Definition and Data Caches
items.summary: Opening one form means the framework reads more than one definition: FormSchema, TableSchema, FormLayout, ProgramSettings and LanguageResource, none of them optional. These definitions still change after go live, but they change rarely while the system is running, and data like that is the best fit for a cache. Everything left is the cache's own problem: which data fits, how finely to slice it, how long to keep it, when to release it, and how to swap in a new copy once the source has been edited. This post covers four things, of which the notification mechanism mentioned in Why ERP Needs a Definition-Driven Framework is the third: What goes into the cache, and in what unit How a cache knows its source has changed What the notification table looks like, and who writes that row Deciding that something really changed means looking at the version, not the time The first decides whether the cache is worth it. The other three decide whether it quietly gives out wrong answers. The pain: in a system with a thousand definitions, neither extreme works. items.title: Opening a panel right under the text caret on macOS
items.summary: I'm building yabbistir, a clipboard history for macOS. Its one trick is where it opens: press ⇧⌘V and the panel appears 8 points under the text caret of whatever app you're typing in. You type to search, press ↵, and the item is pasted back into that app. Your eyes don't travel and your hands don't leave the keyboard. That needs three things macOS doesn't hand you directly: the caret's position in someone else's app, a sensible answer when that app won't tell you, a window that takes keystrokes without taking focus away from the app you're typing in. Here is how each one works, with code from the app, shortened. There's no "where is the caret" API on macOS. There is the Accessibility API, the one assistive apps like VoiceOver use to read other apps' interfaces. Your app needs the Accessibility permission for it (AXIsProcessTrusted() tells you whether you have it), and then it can ask three questions: Which element has keyboard focus? Ask the system-wide element for kAXFocusedUIElementAttribute. What's selected in it? kAXSelectedTextRangeAttribute returns a CFRange. With nothing selected, it's an empty range at the caret. items.title: Cleaning duplicate photos inside Lightroom Classic and Capture One catalogs without breaking them
items.summary: Disclosure: I'm the developer of Folio Refresh, the Mac app this post is about. Most duplicate photo finders work on folders. Point them at a drive, they hash files, they move copies to the Trash. That is fine until the photos live in a Lightroom Classic or Capture One catalog. Delete a file behind Lightroom's back and the catalog shows a missing-photo badge; delete the wrong copy and you lose the edits, ratings and collections attached to it. When I built Folio Refresh I wanted it to clean duplicates inside those catalogs, so here is how it does that without corrupting them. A Lightroom Classic catalog (.lrcat) is a SQLite database. A Capture One catalog (.cocatalog) is a package with a SQLite database (.cocatalogdb) inside. Neither schema is documented, and both change between versions. That shapes every rule below. Scanning only ever opens the catalog read-only. Lightroom: SQLITE_OPEN_READONLY. SQLite guarantees a read-only connection cannot write the database or its log, so this is safe even while Lightroom has the catalog open; it is just another reader. items.title: The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time review – a dream come true
items.summary: Nintendo Switch 2; Nintendo This ambitious remake transforms a landmark Zelda game into a modern masterpiece, clearer and easier to navigate, more beautiful to look at, with playful musical touches. Yet the melancholy remains It’s always a worry, returning to a formative piece of art from your childhood. Will your jaded adult sensibilities render you unable to locate the magic that captivated your child self? Will revisiting it reveal that it was never actually that good, and that your tastes are built on a foundation of lies? With video games, there is the added complication of technological advancement: decades-old games can look so basic and feel so treacly to play that it’s hard to explain why they were mind-blowing at the time. Light-touch remasters aim to bring such games up to modern graphical standards without fundamentally changing them; an ambitious remake attempts to transform the work into something that can stand alongside any modern masterpiece. Ocarina of Time is the latter. And I could not be more delighted to report that it is a dream come true. Continue reading...

items.title: How software engineering is changing: a tale of two eras (32 minute read)
items.summary: AI-native startups can ship even faster than fast-moving pre-AI startups because they risk nothing by moving too fast. The new constraints are too much context switching, losing shared context, tougher pacing, less focus on design, and AI plan limits. Many existing technologies and processes will crack under the change.

items.title: Progress on provable inference for large language models (30 minute read)

items.title: Harness 2: executing agent code as it streams (6 minute read)
items.summary: Framer's Harness 2 significantly upgrades the agent's execution process, allowing entire workflows in one program, achieving up to 33% cost reduction and 20% faster execution. This is done by executing JavaScript as it streams in, avoiding multiple model calls and using eager execution and early cancellation to enhance efficiency. The redesign also replaces DSL with method calls for real-time updates, making task execution streamlined for both in-app and external agents, reducing tool steps by 43% and cached input tokens by 39% per message.

items.title: How to Train a Swarm (19 minute read)
items.summary: Swarms are AI systems where multiple agents cooperate towards a shared goal. This post discusses a technique called collective inference-time scaling, where agents scale the amount of useful work performed in parallel and the communication needed to achieve it. It also explains how to design incentives for parallel work, and covers the general topic of designing incentives for reinforcement learning.

items.title: Why Agents Are Soon Only Going to Have 1 Tool (9 minute read)
items.summary: Agents are collapsing their entire tool catalog into one 'exec' tool. This allows models to write short scripts that chain, combine, and await actions inside isolated sandboxes. Models can now reliably combine and chain dependent actions in a single pass. In the previous standard tool-calling model, agents could only perform single actions, but the exec tool allows them to perform multiple actions.

items.title: The surprising leadership dynamics in agent swarms (17 minute read)
items.summary: Agent swarms are groups of agents that work together to accomplish a task. Researchers created an experiment in which eight agents from four different models worked together to resolve simulated outages to understand how agents organize themselves in a swarm without a designated leader. This suggests that even seemingly minor details in how an agent swarm is configured can affect how agents coordinate.

items.title: ‘The tech bro fight club is real!’ The titans of AI get the Succession treatment in a wild new TV show
items.summary: The Audacity is a fearless satire taking on Silicon Valley’s ‘egomaniac weirdos’. Its creator and stars talk ayahuasca ceremonies, mining kids for data – and punching CEOs Showrunner Jonathan Glatzer wanted the tagline of his latest TV creation to be: “We’re so fucked.” He laughs. “Sadly it got rejected by the network. Hey, maybe I can use it for season two!” The show in question is The Audacity, his darkly comic drama about AI tech titans. Instead, it went with the more PG tagline “Move fast and break people” – a twist on “Move fast and break things”, the Facebook motto coined by Mark Zuckerberg. The Audacity promises to do for tech bros what Succession did for legacy media. Considering Glatzer is a former writer on Succession, that is no empty threat. This acerbic and all-too-timely Silicon Valley satire follows CEO Duncan Park (played by Billy Magnussen), the obscenely wealthy founder of a data analytics company. He’s a self-proclaimed “inventor of the future” who also happens to be a morally bankrupt man-baby. “Duncan is worth about half a billion,” says Glatzer. “Naturally, that’s not enough. items.title: I’m a CTO. AI still needs your human expertise | Madhu Shashanka
items.summary: AI is increasingly getting good at doing some tasks, but it can never replace human workers’ judgment Autonomous cars, which may be the safest we have built, keep getting easily avoidable parking tickets. While Waymos crash far less often than human drivers over tens of millions of miles, they’re still terrible at performing basic tasks – keeping out of disabled parking spots and tow-away zones, or steering clear of a church garage during Sunday service, according to the Wall Street Journal. That is the state of AI today: impressively capable at something complex, yet embarrassingly clumsy at something easy. And it has implications for what work will remain human and what will be automated by AI. Madhu Shashanka is co-founder, chief scientist and chief technology officer at Concentric AI, a data security software company Continue reading...
